extracted.intended_audience: general readers and mathematicians interested in the Clay Mathematics Institute's Millennium Prize Problems
extracted.subtask_description: Official statements and descriptions of the seven Clay Mathematics Institute Millennium Prize Problems and the basic awarding condition; summarizes the formal problem formulations and any specific requirements (e.g., required axiomatic properties) mentioned on the page.

rubrics_metrics.name: Millennium Prize award condition
rubrics_metrics.description: The Clay Institute has pledged to pay one million US dollars for the first correct solution to each problem; the seven problems were officially designated 'Millennium Problems' by the Clay Mathematics Institute.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Award is to the first correct solution as judged by the Institute; historical note: Grigori Perelman was awarded the prize for the Poincaré conjecture in 2010 but declined the award. The page does not reproduce the full procedural rules for verification/eligibility used by the Clay Institute.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poincaré conjecture (official statement)
rubrics_metrics.description: Any three-dimensional topological manifold which is closed and simply-connected must be homeomorphic to the 3-sphere.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Equivalent formulations exist in the smooth category (smooth manifolds and diffeomorphisms). The page notes a proof was given by Grigori Perelman (2002–2003) completing Hamilton's Ricci flow program; methods revolve around Ricci flow (a system of PDEs in Riemannian geometry). The Clay Institute awarded the Millennium Prize for this solution (which Perelman declined).

rubrics_metrics.name: Birch and Swinnerton-Dyer conjecture (Millennium version)
rubrics_metrics.description: For an elliptic curve E over the rational numbers with rank r, the associated L-function L(E,s) vanishes to order r at s = 1.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the Clay Institute's formal/Millennium version of the conjecture; the page attributes the official statement to Andrew Wiles. The entry summarizes the conjecture's domain (elliptic curves over Q) and what constitutes the asserted relationship between rank and the behavior of the L-function at s=1.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hodge conjecture (official statement)
rubrics_metrics.description: For projective algebraic varieties, Hodge cycles are rational linear combinations of algebraic cycles. Modern statement: Let X be a non-singular complex projective variety. Then every Hodge class on X is a linear combination with rational coefficients of the cohomology classes of complex subvarieties of X.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page gives the formal modern formulation and notes Pierre Deligne provided the official statement for the Clay problems volume. This entry records the exact mathematical formulation required to count as a solution to the Hodge conjecture as presented.

rubrics_metrics.name: Navier–Stokes existence and smoothness (official statement)
rubrics_metrics.description: For the three-dimensional incompressible Navier–Stokes system given specified initial conditions, either prove that smooth, globally defined solutions always exist meeting certain conditions, or prove that they do not always exist (i.e., the equations can break down).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page displays the Navier–Stokes PDE and explains the problem’s two-fold nature (global existence and/or finite-time breakdown of smooth solutions). The official statement for the Clay list was given by Charles Fefferman. A valid solution must address the 3D, incompressible case and the required smoothness/existence criteria referenced in the official statement.

rubrics_metrics.name: P versus NP (official statement)
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether every problem whose solutions can be verified in polynomial time (NP) can also be solved in polynomial time (P), i.e., whether P = NP or P ≠ NP.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page frames the question as whether an algorithm that verifies a given solution quickly implies an algorithm that finds such a solution quickly. It gives consequences (implications for mathematics, biology, philosophy, cryptography) and cites Stephen Cook as giving the official statement. Examples such as Boolean satisfiability are mentioned as canonical NP problems not known to be in P.

rubrics_metrics.name: Riemann hypothesis (official statement)
rubrics_metrics.description: All nontrivial zeros of the Riemann zeta function ζ(s) have real part equal to 1/2.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page explains the zeta function, trivial vs nontrivial zeros, and states the hypothesis in the standard form. It notes wide implications for number theory (distribution of prime numbers), historical origin (Riemann, 1859), and that the Clay exposition was given by Enrico Bombieri. A proof or disproof should establish the asserted location of all nontrivial zeros.

rubrics_metrics.name: Yang–Mills existence and mass gap (official statement and axiomatic requirement)
rubrics_metrics.description: Prove that for any compact simple gauge group G, a non-trivial quantum Yang–Mills theory exists on R^4 and has a mass gap Δ > 0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page specifies that 'existence' includes establishing axiomatic properties at least as strong as those cited in Streater & Wightman (1964) and Osterwalder & Schrader (1973, 1975). The entry records both the mass-gap requirement (Δ0 > 0) and the demand that the constructed quantum field theory satisfy rigorous axiomatic properties comparable to the cited literature; the official statement is attributed to Arthur Jaffe and Edward Witten.
